title: From Mutton Biryani to Fish Curry: Indian Temples Where Non-Vegetarian Prasad Is Sacred
excerpt: Across India, centuries-old temples challenge mainstream assumptions about temple food, serving meat, fish, and even liquor as divine offerings rooted in Tantric and tribal traditions.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Several Hindu temples serve non-vegetarian prasad, including mutton biryani and fish curry.
  • These practices stem from ancient Tantric and tribal traditions predating vegetarianism in Hinduism.
  • Temples like Kamakhya and Kalighat attract thousands for their unique meat offerings.
  • Historical texts sanctioned animal sacrifice, with up to 50 animals accepted for rituals.

Based on historical texts and temple practices.
  • Several prominent Hindu temples across India serve non-vegetarian prasad, including mutton biryani, fish curry, and goat meat, as part of centuries-old ritual traditions.
  • The practice is rooted in Tantric worship, Shakti Peetha traditions, and tribal belief systems that predate the dominance of Brahmanical vegetarianism in mainstream Hinduism.
  • Temples such as Kamakhya in Assam, Kalighat in Kolkata, and the Muniyandi Swamy temple in Tamil Nadu draw thousands of devotees for their distinctive non-vegetarian offerings.
  • Historical texts including the Vedas sanctioned animal sacrifice, with food historian K.T. Achaya noting that up to 50 types of animals were acceptable for sacrificial offerings during yajnas.

When most people think of temple prasad in India, images of sweet laddoos, fragrant rice, or simple vegetarian dishes come to mind. But in dozens of temples scattered across the subcontinent, the sacred kitchen tells a very different story — one where goat meat, fried fish, and even country liquor are considered divine offerings.

These traditions, far from being aberrations, are among the oldest forms of Hindu worship in India. They are deeply embedded in Tantric rituals, Shakti Peetha practices, and the tribal customs of communities that have maintained them for centuries, even as mainstream Hinduism moved toward vegetarianism.

Where Meat Meets the Divine

The Kamakhya Temple in Guwahati, Assam, one of India's most powerful Shakti Peethas, is perhaps the best-known example. Dedicated to the goddess of fertility, the temple offers goat meat and fish to the deity during specific hours. The meat is prepared without onion or garlic — ingredients considered impure in this particular ritual context — and is later distributed to devotees as prasad. During the annual Ambubachi Mela, animal sacrifice is a central part of the festivities, according to the Bombay Times.

In Kolkata, the 200-year-old Kalighat Temple — another Shakti Peetha believed to mark the spot where Goddess Sati's right foot fell — continues the practice of goat sacrifice. While Goddess Kali herself is offered vegetarian food, her attendants, the Dakinis and Yoginis, receive the meat. It is then cooked without onion and garlic and distributed as prasadam to devotees.

Further south, the Muniyandi Swamy Temple near Madurai, Tamil Nadu, takes the tradition to an extraordinary scale. During its annual three-day festival honouring Lord Muniyandi — a guardian deity and local form of Shiva — the temple prepares an estimated 2,000 kilograms of chicken and mutton biryani, which is served to thousands of devotees as prasad, according to the Bombay Times.

Liquor, Fish, and Earthen Pots

The Kaal Bhairav Temple in Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh, adds another dimension to these traditions. This 6,000-year-old temple dedicated to a fierce form of Lord Shiva offers alcohol — typically country liquor — to the deity. Devotees pour it into a saucer near the deity's mouth, and what remains is returned as prasad. Local belief holds that the deity visibly "accepts" the offering.

In Kerala, the Parassinikaduvu Muthappan Temple serves toddy and fried fish as offerings to Lord Muthappan, considered a Kali Yuga incarnation of Shiva and Vishnu. Even today, boiled grains, coconut, and fish are offered as prasadam at this shrine.

At the Tarkulha Devi Temple in Gorakhpur, Uttar Pradesh, goat sacrifice is performed during Chaitra Navratri as part of the annual Khichdi Mela. The meat is slow-cooked in traditional earthen pots and served alongside baati as prasad. The tradition is linked to local warrior legends and the story of Amar Shaheed Bandhu Singh.

Ancient Roots, Modern Tensions

These practices have deep historical precedent. The Vedas, dating back to 1500 BCE, sanctioned animal sacrifice as a legitimate ritual act. Food historian K.T. Achaya documented that as many as 50 types of animals were considered acceptable for sacrificial offerings during yajnas, according to the Times of India's food vertical.

Over centuries, the rise of Jainism and Buddhism, along with the increasing dominance of Brahmanical vegetarianism, gradually stigmatised meat consumption in religious contexts. By the 7th century BCE, vegetarianism had become associated with moral purity, and caste hierarchies reinforced this association.

Yet in regions steeped in Shakti worship — Bengal, Assam, parts of Tamil Nadu and Kerala — animal sacrifice persisted as an integral part of devotion. Even Kashmiri Pandits historically included fish and lamb in religious feasts, a practice shaped by the harsh climate that limited vegetable availability during winter months.

A Diaspora Connection

For members of the Indian diaspora, these traditions offer a window into the extraordinary diversity of Hindu practice that often goes unrecognised abroad. While temple food in diaspora communities tends toward the vegetarian mainstream, these non-vegetarian traditions remind us that Indian spirituality has never been monolithic.

The Dakshineswar Kali Temple in Kolkata, the Tarapith Temple in Birbhum, and the Rajrappa Temple in Jharkhand all continue to serve fish and meat as bhog — traditions that remain vibrant, unapologetic, and deeply sacred to the communities that sustain them.

What's Next

As debates around food, identity, and religious purity intensify in contemporary India, these temples stand as living evidence of a more pluralistic spiritual past. Their survival challenges the notion that Hindu worship was ever uniformly vegetarian — and suggests that faith, like food, resists reduction to a single recipe.
